title: Pitfalls in the diagnosis of new-onset frontal lobe seizures☆
case_prompt: A 22-year-old right-handed woman was referred for several weekly episodes of paroxysmal motor behaviors and a possible generalized tonic–clonic seizure. Each stereotyped episode began with tonic elevation and abduction of the right arm, sometimes followed by right leg movements. Birth, developmental, and medical histories were unremarkable, and there was no family history of epilepsy. Neurological examination was normal. Brain MRI and routine interictal EEG were interpreted as normal. Because of the suspected unprovoked tonic–clonic seizure, oxcarbazepine was started; the stereotyped movements decreased but persisted. A neurologist who witnessed an episode diagnosed psychogenic nonepileptic seizures and antiepileptic treatment was progressively withdrawn. Shortly after cessation, she experienced clusters of similar paroxysmal motor events followed by probable generalized tonic–clonic seizures and was referred to our department. On arrival, she was awake, alert, and her neurological examination remained normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. A generalized tonic–clonic seizure was initially suspected — “The suspicion of an initial unprovoked generalized tonic–clonic seizure led to a first antiepileptic treatment with oxcarbazepine.”
2. Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures were considered due to paroxysmal behavioral and emotional changes without EEG confirmation but later excluded because “postictal acute and fast-resolving psychotic features have, indeed, never been reported as a complication of PNES.”
3. Temporal lobe epilepsy was contemplated given that “postictal psychosis is … more often present … especially temporal lobe epilepsy” but was deemed unlikely when video-EEG revealed seizure activity “predominating in the midline frontocentral electrodes (Fz, Cz).”
4. A primary psychiatric disorder was considered because “both epilepsy and PNES present high comorbidity with psychiatric disorders,” but was ruled out when the patient’s “psychotic symptoms disappeared within 24 h,” consistent with a postictal phenomenon.
5. Frontal lobe epilepsy was confirmed by subtle ictal EEG correlates in prefrontal regions — “ictal EEG revealed very discrete abnormalities … 1 to 3 s before the clinical onset … followed by a focal theta (4 c/s) rhythmic activity … in the same electrodes.”
